newsitem.title: DUBAI: Ex-Dubai air cargo rates static in slow '97 start.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Dubai air cargo rates static in slow '97 start.

text.p: Most air cargo operators in Dubai are relieved 1996 is over and are holding out for a better 1997, with stronger volumes and more success in meeting sales targets, a Reuters survey showed

Even though total cargo volumes at the airport rose 14 percent in the year to a record 358,982 tonnes, due mainly to a 17 percent increase in imports, airlines said the rise was not enough to counter increases in cargo capacity during the year.
"The pie might be a bit bigger, but there are more people fighting over it," said one airline manager, adding the rise was mainly in transhipment rather than Dubai-sourced freight.
"It's been really difficult to meet sales targets," said a cargo executive, echoing the sentiments shared by many others.
Transhipment business during the year was good, rising 23 percent, with air-to-air shipments gaining greater importance at the expense of sea-air movements, which fell four percent.
But so far, 1997 has provided little to be positive about and cargo industry sources said rates are steady at their mid-December levels, apart from those to east Africa.
"The market is very quiet. There are dribs and drabs, but the whole of December and the first few weeks of January have been slow," said the cargo representative of a large European carrier.

"The Dubai-originating market has not firmed up yet and we are relying on traffic from the Indian subcontinent and the Far East to Europe," said a cargo executive of a carrier dominant in the ex-Dubai market.
The start of the Islamic month of Ramadan, when Moslems fast during the day and work shorter hours, has not helped.
"It's an excuse for freight forwarders to relax and this affects the trade. They are not at full speed," said one.
The shorter hours were also affecting production in the country's textile sector, which this week received U.S. quotas for exports, industry executives said.
"Production is limited, the level has dropped. The quota has been released, but at the wrong time of the year (Ramadan)," one said.

"The (garments) stock from 1996 is over and production is very low profile at the moment because it is the beginning of the year and Ramadan. We hope it will pick up in mid-February," commented a forwarder.

At the start of each year Washington allocates quotas to various countries giving the amount of textiles it is prepared to import from them in the year. The local authorities then decide how much of the quota each textile manufacturer will get.
"The full allotment was released yesterday so maybe we will see some large movement in the next couple of weeks," said one cargo manager.
"Out of Dubai the textile movement will start only after two or three months," said another. "By the end of February it will be gradually increasing," he added.

Reuters calculates the average rate on a 100 kg shipment with a six-to-one volume-to-weight ratio to London Heathrow static at 4.05 dirhams per kilo. The same average rate, which includes the fuel surcharge introduced by most airlines late last year, applies to Frankfurt.
Dubai-Nairobi rates are the only movers -- climbing to an average 4.15 dirhams on a 100 kg shipment from 4.00 dirhams per kilo a month ago.

"Business to east Africa is brisk. Ramadan is not keeping the African traders away," said an agent, adding that all sorts of cargo, included unbranded electronics, children's clothes and textiles were destined for Nairobi, Entebbe and Dar es Salaam.
"It's anything and everything."
The rates to New York and Los Angeles have remained unchanged. The average rate to JFK is 6.45 dirhams a kg and the rate to Los Angeles is at 7.50 dirhams.
Rates on Far East routes are also steady, after a small rise in December on seasonal demand for space for perishables. The average is 4.00 to both Singapore and Hong Kong.
While business to east Africa is encouraging, the outlook for the rest of the market is less bright.
"Out of Dubai there is no room for an increase in rates in at least the next two to three months," said one cargo manager.

"With the Chinese New Year coming up in the Far East we can expect production there to come to a standstill for about a month. This will affect our business further down the line, especially sea-air," said an agent.
